client: I got promoted a few weeks ago, and honestly, I thought I'd feel happy about it, but instead I just feel completely overwhelmed all the time. Everyone around me seems to think I deserved it, but I keep waiting for someone to figure out that I made a mistake taking this role. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, because the work is still going to be there no matter what.
therapist: What you're describing — that gap between what you expected to feel and what you actually feel — sounds really disorienting, and even though your words carry some uncertainty, your voice tells me there's a quiet but real heaviness underneath all of this. What you're experiencing has a name: it's often called impostor syndrome, and it's incredibly common after a promotion, where your mind starts generating "what if I don't belong here" thoughts that feel like facts even when the evidence — like everyone around you believing you deserved this — points in a very different direction. And I hear your skepticism about whether talking will help, which is a completely valid thought to have, but I'd gently invite you to consider: is it possible that the overwhelm itself is worth exploring, separate from the workload?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I've heard of impostor syndrome before, and I guess it kind of fits, but hearing you name it doesn't automatically make it feel less real, you know? And honestly, I'm not sure I even understand what you mean by exploring the overwhelm separately — it feels like the overwhelm IS the workload, they're the same thing to me.
therapist: You're absolutely right that naming something doesn't make it disappear, and I don't want to minimize that — and I notice there's something in the way you're speaking, a kind of quiet urgency, like you're carrying a lot while trying to hold it together. What I mean by separating the overwhelm from the workload is this: the work itself is real, but the thought "I have to pretend I know what I'm doing" is worth pausing on — because *pretending* implies you don't actually belong there, and I'd want to gently challenge whether that's a fact or a fear your mind has decided to treat as one. What would it look like to walk in tomorrow not as someone pretending, but as someone who is still learning the role they genuinely earned?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe it, but honestly the word "earned" just kind of bounces off me right now. therapist: The way you're speaking right now — fast, loud, with a real intensity behind it — tells me this fear isn't just a passing worry, it's something that's been building pressure inside you, and that makes complete sense given what you're carrying. But I want to gently point out the trap in the thought "if I mess something up, that proves the fear right" — because that's actually an unfalsifiable belief, meaning your mind has set up a system where only perfection counts as evidence you belong, and any mistake becomes proof you don't, which is an exhausting and impossible standard to hold yourself to. What if a mistake tomorrow actually just proved that you're a human being in a new role — the same conclusion we'd draw about literally anyone else in your position?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, very rapid speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and intellectually I can kind of see the logic in it, but it doesn't really land emotionally for me. Like, I know other people are allowed to make mistakes in new roles, but when I picture myself doing it, it just feels different, more permanent somehow, like people will remember it and it'll follow me. And honestly the "you're just human" reframe feels a little too easy, like it lets me off the hook in a way that doesn't match how high the stakes actually feel at this job.
therapist: There's something really telling in the way you just said that — your voice was soft, almost careful, like you were choosing your words precisely because this matters deeply to you, and I want to honor that rather than offer you another reframe that slides off. You've actually identified something important: the belief that *your* mistakes are different, more permanent, more defining than other people's — and that's worth sitting with, because it tells us this isn't really about logic at all, it's about a deeper conviction you hold about yourself that no amount of clever reframing will touch until we start examining where that belief actually comes from. Can you tell me more about that sense of permanence — has there been a time before this job where a mistake felt like it followed you in the way you're describing?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: Yeah, there was this one time in college where I failed an exam that I should have passed, and I told myself I'd just move on, but honestly I carried that feeling of being a fraud all the way through graduation. It wasn't even a big deal objectively, but it became this kind of proof in my head that I was always going to fall short when it really counted. And now with this job situation, it feels like that same proof is just getting confirmed again, like the evidence is stacking up against me.
therapist: The way you're speaking right now — fast, loud, with a real urgency — tells me this memory still carries a lot of weight, even as you're trying to lay it out calmly, and what you've just shared is actually really significant. You've described a pattern where your mind took one painful moment and quietly promoted it into a life sentence — "I will always fall short when it really counts" — and now every new challenge, including this promotion, gets filtered through that same lens, so the evidence only ever stacks one way. What strikes me is that your mind has been a very loyal keeper of that old story, but I'd gently ask: has there been *any* moment between that exam and today where you didn't fall short when it counted — because if so, that evidence belongs in the pile too.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, very rapid speech

client: I mean... yeah, there probably have been moments, but it feels almost dishonest to count them, you know? Like, the promotion is so much bigger than those smaller wins, so they don't really feel like they belong in the same category. And I guess part of me is worried that if I start believing I can handle it, and then I fail anyway, that's going to hurt so much worse than just expecting the worst from the start.
therapist: The softness in your voice just now, almost tentative, like you were carefully admitting something you hadn't quite said out loud before, tells me that last part was really important — because what you've just described isn't really about the promotion at all, it's about self-protection, keeping your hopes small so the fall hurts less. That's such an understandable strategy, and it makes complete sense given how much that college experience cost you emotionally, but I want to gently name what it's actually doing: it's asking you to pay the full price of failure *in advance*, every single day, as a kind of insurance against future pain. What if hope and preparation aren't the same as naivety — and what if allowing yourself to count those smaller wins isn't dishonest, but actually the more accurate picture of who you are?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

therapist: The way you're speaking right now — very fast, soft, with a kind of tightness in your voice — tells me that even saying this out loud feels risky, like you're moving carefully around something that still has real power to hurt you, and I want you to know that what you just named, that vulnerability feels like danger, is one of the most honest and important things you've said today. You're not resisting the reframe because you're being stubborn — you're resisting it because the last time you trusted yourself, it felt like the ground gave way, and your mind learned a very reasonable lesson from that. I'm not asking you to leap into vulnerability all at once; I'm just wondering if we could start somewhere smaller — not "I trust myself completely," but maybe just "I'm willing to stay curious about whether the old story is the whole story."

therapist: There's something quietly significant happening right now — your voice is soft and quick, almost like you're thinking out loud in real time, and the fact that something *didn't* land badly for you is actually worth pausing on, because that small opening is exactly what curiosity looks like in practice.
